notes/implemented-network-defenses.html.title: Implemented Network Defenses
notes/implemented-network-defenses.html.description:
I learned how to protect network infrastructure by designing, deploying, and validating security controls across both on-premises and cloud environments. Repurposing 32-bit Laptop as Linux Firewall for Cybersecurity Lab - Configured a default-deny stateful firewall using nftables to control local lab traffic and implemented DNS sinkholing to block specified domains.
Bridging Lab to the Cloud with Site-to-Site VPN - Extended network defenses by securing an encrypted WireGuard tunnel and applying strict routing policies between the on-premises lab and AWS environment.
Developing Wazuh Decoders and Rules for Lab Firewall - Validated these network defenses by simulating port scans and packet floods, ensuring malicious traffic was properly dropped, logged, and flagged by the SIEM.

Also known as Public Law No: 113-274Titled Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity, issued on Feb 2013 due to increasing cyber threats to critical infrastructure. It focuses on three areas: information sharing privacy adoption of cybersecurity practices National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) was directed to develop a cybersecurity framework from existing voluntary consensus standards and industry best practices. Titled Strengthening the Cybersecurity of Federal Networks and Critical Infrastructure, issued on May 2017. Mandates the framework for all government agencies Still voluntary for everyone else Requires agencies to: Inventory computer systems Identify and provide appropriate security protections Develop, document, and implement agency-wide information security program Intended to reduce cracking of computer systems and to address federal computer-related offenses. notes/understanding-of-event-logs.html.title: Understanding of Event Logs
notes/understanding-of-event-logs.html.description:
By managing the full lifecycle of event logs. I learned how telemetry provides critical visibility into network health and security. Repurposing 32-bit Laptop as Linux Firewall for Cybersecurity Lab - Configured rsyslog to parse and separate raw service logs into dedicated files, and implemented logrotate to prevent disk exhaustion over time.
Bridging Lab to the Cloud with Site-to-Site VPN - Architected a secure logging pipeline to transport local network telemetry to the Wazuh SIEM hosted in the AWS cloud.
Developing Wazuh Decoders and Rules for Lab Firewall - Analyzed unstructured firewall logs and wrote custom PCRE2 decoders to extract specific data fields (like source IP, destination port, and query type) for behavioral alert mapping.

Working extensively via the command-line interface (CLI) across multiple projects allowed me to build a practical understanding of Linux operating systems. Repurposing 32-bit Laptop as Linux Firewall for Cybersecurity Lab - Deployed a headless AntiX OS, navigate through the file system, modified application and network interfaces configuration files, and managed sysVinit services entirely through the CLI.
Bridging Lab to the Cloud with Site-to-Site VPN - Provisioned and administered Linux-based AWS EC2 instances, generating SSH keys and managing secure remote connections.
Developing Wazuh Decoders and Rules for Lab Firewall - Navigated into Linux (ubuntu) file systems, modify SIEM's XML configuration files, and manage backend services directly from the terminal.

Bridging Lab to the Cloud with Site-to-Site VPN - Implemented static routing and configured network policies to successfully establish a Site-to-Site VPN connecting the on-premises network to an AWS Virtual Private Cloud (VPC).

projects/bridging-lab-to-the-cloud-with-.title: Bridging Lab to the Cloud with Site-to-Site VPN
projects/bridging-lab-to-the-cloud-with-.description:
{ "type": "project", "spec": [ { "name": "cloud", "rank": 9, "description": "Integrated the home lab with AWS by deploying a site-to-site WireGuard VPN, configuring VPC routing, Security Groups, and nftables to securely extend the lab into a cloud environment." }, { "name": "cybersecurity", "rank": 9, "description": "Implemented secure connectivity between on-premises and cloud networks using network segmentation, least-privilege firewall policies, and centralized security monitoring through Wazuh." } ] } Date: Jun 24, 2026 Tags: Network Security Cloud Infrastructure Log Management System Administration SIEM AWS Security Group Wazuh Firewall WireGuard nftables tcpdump netcat iperf nftables Linux
Collecting event logs in a centralized location is important for network visibility and incident response. However, as infrastructure expands to remote branches and into the cloud, transmitting traffic over the public internet introduces risks of interception from threat actors.To address this, I established a site-to-site VPN using WireGuard to connect the Lab network directly to my AWS cloud environment. This encrypted tunnel will be used to transport logs and access the Wazuh SIEM without exposing the web management ports to the public internet. This builds on top of the previous entry where I turned an AntiX Linux host into a firewall and DNS sinkhole.
Established an encrypted communication tunnel between lab and remote infrastructures by implementing a site-to-site VPN using WireGuard. This adds an extra layer of protection when sending important data through the internet. Established a Secured Site-to-Site VPN Solution I chose WireGuard primarily as it is lighter compared to other common VPN protocols like IPsec and OpenVPN. This is important as WireGuard will be running on the AntiX Firewall that has 32-bit CPU. The tunnel will also be used to access Wazuh Dashboard and management ports. Lab firewall: 1 [Interface] 2 Address = 172.16.99.1/24 3 SaveConfig = false 4 ListenPort = 51820 5 PrivateKey = <LAB-FW_PRIVATE-KEY> 6 7 [Peer] 8 PublicKey = <AWS-GW_PUBLIC-KEY> 9 Endpoint = <AWS-GW_PUBLIC-IP>:51820 10 AllowedIPs = 172.31.20.233/32, 172.31.11.191/32, 172.16.99.2/32 11 PersistentKeepalive = 25 AWS Gateway: 1 [Interface] 2 Address = 172.16.99.2/24 3 SaveConfig = false 4 ListenPort = 51820 5 PrivateKey = <AWS-GW_PRIVATE-KEY> 6 MTU = 1420 7 8 [Peer] 9 PublicKey = <LAB-FW_PUBLIC-KEY> 10 AllowedIPs = 172.16.99.1/32 I enabled NAT on traffic from lab network going to AWS Gateway via the encrypted tunnel. AWS instances would only see the (AntiX) Lab Firewall 172.16.99.1 as source of all traffic. This simplifies routing but relies on the Lab Firewall to apply strict security policies.
Simplified Routing Tables on AWS On the (AntiX) Lab Firewall, On postrouting chain, only traffic destined to AWS gateway or Wazuh Server will be source-NATed to Lab Router IP (172.16.99.1) (See line 102). 1 flush ruleset 2 3 # Interfaces 4 define wireguard = "wg0" 5 define lan = "lan0" 6 define wan = "wan0" 7 8 # Addresses 9 define gateway_public_ip = { 18.138.54.108 } 10 define gateway_private_ip = { 172.31.11.191 } ... 98 chain postrouting { 99 type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; policy accept; 100 101 oifname $wan masquerade 102 oifname $wireguard ip daddr { $gateway_private_ip, $wazuh_ip} masquerade 103 } Since AWS Gateway will act mainly as a WireGuard peer, I only allowed wg_port so that Lab Firewall can initiate a connection, ICMP request from lab for troubleshooting, and SSH from lab for management. It will only forward traffic used by Wazuh services. 1 #!/usr/sbin/nft -f 2 3 flush ruleset 4 # -- Interfaces -- 5 define pub_iface = "ens5" 6 define wg_iface = "wg0" 7 # -- Target IPs -- 8 define wazuh_ip = { 172.31.20.233 } 9 define lab_ip = { 172.16.99.1 } 10 # -- Ports -- 11 define ssh_ports = { 22 } 12 define wazuh_ports = { 1514, 1515, 443 } 13 define syslog_ports = { 514 } 14 define wg_port = 51820 15 16 table inet filter { 17 chain input { 18 type filter hook input priority filter; policy drop; 19 iif "lo" accept 20 ct state established,related accept 21 ct state invalid drop 22 icmp type echo-request accept 23 iifname $pub_iface udp dport $wg_port accept 24 iifname $wg_iface ip saddr $lab_ip tcp dport $ssh_ports accept 25 } 26 27 chain forward { 28 type filter hook forward priority filter; policy drop; 29 ct state established,related accept 30 ct state invalid drop 31 icmp type echo-request accept 32 33 iifname $wg_iface ip daddr $wazuh_ip tcp dport { $wazuh_ports, $syslog_ports, $ssh_ports } accept 34 iifname $wg_iface ip daddr $wazuh_ip udp dport { $wazuh_ports } accept 35 } 36 } I also updated the security group of Wazuh Server to only accept through the intended ports. (Antix) Lab Firewall IP is still visible because sNAT is not enabled on the AWS Gateway. This allows Security Group to give different access level for different VPN peers. In order for return traffic to arrive, I set up a route on the VPC: Applied strict filtering on the lab firewall by specifying which hosts or networks have access to which remote servers and services. This filters the invalid traffic before it leaves the network which saves bandwidth and adds an extra layer of security. Implementing Layered Security (nftables & WireGuard) On AntiX Firewall, I specified which protocol/ports are allowed to be forwarded to Wazuh. Then allowed SSH and HTTPS from admin IP only. While admin IP can be spoofed, SSH to aws instances still requires ssh key file. Then, to implement SNAT on traffic going out of wireguard interface (See line 99). 1 flush ruleset 2 3 # Interfaces 4 define wireguard = "wg0" 5 define lan = "lan0" 6 define wan = "wan0" 7 8 # Addresses 9 define gateway_public_ip = { 18.138.54.108 } 10 define gateway_private_ip = { 172.31.11.191 } 11 define gateway_wireguard_ip = { 172.16.99.2 } 12 define wazuh_ip = { 172.31.20.233 } 13 define admin_ip = { 10.0.0.50 } 14 define blocked_ip = { 9.9.9.9 } 15 16 # Ports 17 define dns_ports = { 53 } 18 define web_ports = { 80,443 } 19 define ntp_ports = { 123 } 20 define ssh_ports = { 22 } 21 define wazuh_ports = { 1514,1515 } 22 define syslog_ports = { 514 } 23 define vpn_ports = { 51820 } 24 25 define common_tcp_ports = { 53,80,443 } 26 define common_udp_ports = { 53,123 } 27 28 # FILTER TABLE 29 table inet filter { ... 44 chain forward { 45 type filter hook forward priority filter; policy drop; 46 ct state established,related accept 47 ct state invalid log prefix "NFT-FOR-DROP-INVALID " drop 48 ip daddr $blocked_ip log prefix "NFT-FOR-DROP-QUAD9 " drop 49 iifname $lan oifname $wan tcp dport $common_tcp_ports accept 50 iifname $lan oifname $wan udp dport $common_udp_ports accept 51 iifname $lan oifname $wireguard ip daddr $wazuh_ip tcp dport $wazuh_ports accept 52 ip saddr $admin_ip ip daddr { $gateway_private_ip, $wazuh_ip } tcp dport 22 accept 53 ip saddr $admin_ip ip daddr $wazuh_ip tcp dport 443 accept 54 icmp type echo-request accept 55 log prefix "NFT-FOR-DROP-DEFAULT " 56 } ... 87 table ip nat { ... 95 chain postrouting { 96 type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; policy accept; 97 98 oifname $wan masquerade 99 oifname $wireguard masquerade 100 } 101 } AntiX firewall will also accept traffic only if they are intended to Wazuh Server (172.31.20.233) or AWS Gateway (172.16.99.2 / 172.31.11.191). Even if the nftables break, there is another layer of security before it gets tunneled to AWS Gateway. 10 AllowedIPs = 172.31.20.233/32, 172.31.11.191/32, 172.16.99.2/32 File: /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf (Lab Firewall) Deployed a security information and event management (SIEM) system that collects telemetry from various endpoints and devices. This provides better visibility on overall security posture, improves threat detection, and incident response. Deploying Endpoint Detection and Response Agent While I can just install a Wazuh agent on AntiX firewall, I want to set it up as a real network device where installing an agent is not an option. So I emulated how they would transfer their traffic with rsyslog on the AntiX Firewall (see Line 3 & 8). 1 # 1. Capture Firewall logs 2 :msg, contains, "NFT-" /var/log/nftables.log 3 action(type="omfwd" target="172.31.20.233" port="514" protocol="tcp") 4 stop 5 6 # 2. Capture all DNS queries 7 if ($syslogtag == 'dnsmasq_log') then { 8 action(type="omfwd" target="172.31.20.233" port="514" protocol="tcp") 9 /var/log/dns.log 10 stop 11 } File: /etc/rsyslog.d/10-firewall.conf (Lab Firewall) I also added a syslog/TCP remote on Wazuh and specified to only accept logs from the Lab Firewall IP. 10 <alerts_log>yes</alerts_log> 11 <logall>yes</logall> 12 <logall_json>yes</logall_json> 13 <email_notification>no</email_notification> ... 41 <remote> 42 <connection>syslog</connection> 43 <port>514</port> 44 <protocol>tcp</protocol> 45 <allowed-ips>172.16.99.1/32</allowed-ips> 46 <local_ip>172.31.20.233</local_ip> 47 </remote> File: /var/ossec/etc/ossec.conf (Wazuh Server) I also installed Wazuh Agent one of the Linux Machine from the lab.
According to the test summary below, the site-to-site VPN implementation was able to bridge the lab network to the remote AWS infrastructure. I also verified that while WireGuard places additional load on the legacy 32-bit CPU, it is not heavy enough to cause bandwidth drops and overheating.Bandwidth & Load Test Summary:Network Access Test Summary:Bandwidth Test (Tunneled v External) Baseline:

projects/repurposing-32-bit-laptop-as-li.title: Repurposing 32-bit Laptop as Linux Firewall for Cybersecurity Lab
projects/repurposing-32-bit-laptop-as-li.description:
Date: Jun 14, 2026 Tags: Network Security System Administration Hardware Troubleshooting Firewall DNS Sinkhole Log Management Linux nftables rsyslog { "type": "project", "spec": [ { "name": "cybersecurity", "rank": 9, "description": "Repurposed a retired 32-bit laptop into a Linux-based firewall for a small cybersecurity lab. Using AntiX Linux, nftables, dnsmasq, rsyslog, and logrotate, the firewall provides network address translation (NAT), stateful packet filtering, DNS sinkholing, and centralized logging." }, { "name": "it-support", "rank": 7, "description": "Extended the usability of legacy 32-bit laptop by upgrading hardware components, installing a lightweight operating system, and configuring the device as a firewall host." } ] }
This project repurposed a retired 32-bit laptop into a Linux-based firewall for a small cybersecurity lab. Using AntiX Linux, nftables, dnsmasq, rsyslog, and logrotate, the firewall provides network address translation (NAT), stateful packet filtering, DNS sinkholing, and centralized logging. The implementation was validated through connectivity, domain-blocking, and traffic-filtering tests while addressing challenges associated with aging hardware and limited resources.
The default policy on all chains under the inet filter was set to drop following a zero trust approach where all connections are denied unless explicitly allowed. Configured Zero-Trust Default-Drop Policy The logging prefix on my config will follow the pattern NFT-[CHAIN]-[ACTION]-[KEYWORD] to make logs easier to analyze and because the action is not included on nftables logs by default. 1 flush ruleset 2 3 table inet filter { 4 chain input { 5 type filter hook input priority filter; policy drop; 6 iif "lo" accept 7 ct state established,related accept 8 ct state invalid log prefix "NFT-IN-DROP-INVALID " drop 9 ip saddr 10.0.0.50 tcp dport 22 accept 10 tcp dport 53 accept 11 udp dport 53 accept 12 icmp type { echo-reply, echo-request } accept 13 log prefix "NFT-IN-DROP-DEFAULT " 14 } 15 16 chain forward { 17 type filter hook forward priority filter; policy drop; 18 ct state established,related accept 19 ct state invalid log prefix "NFT-FOR-DROP-INVALID " drop 20 ip daddr 9.9.9.9 log prefix "NFT-FOR-DROP-QUAD9 " drop 21 tcp dport { 80, 443 } accept 22 udp dport { 53, 123 } accept 23 icmp type { echo-reply, echo-request } accept 24 log prefix "NFT-FOR-DROP-DEFAULT " 25 } 26 27 chain output { 28 type filter hook output priority filter; policy drop; 29 ct state established,related accept 30 ct state invalid log prefix "NFT-OUT-DROP-INVALID " drop 31 hour "17:00"-"04:00" tcp dport { 80, 443, 53 } log prefix "NFT-OUT-ACCEPT-OFFHOUR_TRAFFIC " accept 32 hour "17:00"-"04:00" udp dport { 53, 123 } log prefix "NFT-OUT-ACCEPT-OFFHOUR_TRAFFIC " accept 33 tcp dport { 53, 80, 443 } accept 34 udp dport { 53, 123 } accept 35 icmp type { echo-reply, echo-request } accept 36 log prefix "NFT-OUT-DROP-DEFAULT " 37 } 38 } 39 table ip nat { 40 chain prerouting { 41 type nat hook prerouting priority dstnat; policy accept; 42 iifname "lan0" udp dport 53 dnat to 172.16.0.1 43 iifname "lan0" tcp dport 53 dnat to 172.16.0.1 44 } 45 46 chain postrouting { 47 type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; policy accept; 48 oifname "wan0" masquerade 49 } 50 } File: /etc/nftables.conf The firewall intercepts and redirects all DNS queries to dnsmasq to prevent users from bypassing DNS policies by using external DNS servers. This ensures that blocked domains are not accessible on the internal lab hosts. Blocked Users' Access to Specified Domains For testing purposes, I blocked the domain chess.com. 1 # DNS sinkhole list 2 address=/chess.com/ File: /ect/dnsmasq.d/blocklist.conf I intercepted all DNS queries using the nftables.conf via the prerouting chain. Hosts that modified their computer's DNS servers would still be redirected to the DNS sinkhole. 40 chain prerouting { 41 type nat hook prerouting priority dstnat; policy accept; 42 iifname "lan0" udp dport 53 dnat to 172.16.0.1 43 iifname "lan0" tcp dport 53 dnat to 172.16.0.1 44 } File: /etc/nftables.conf
Disabling the NAT on the Lab Router makes the true source IP addresses visible on the firewall. This allows better visibility and control over the traffic entering and exiting the lab environment. Preserving the True Source IP of Lab Host I disabled the NAT on the Lab Router so that source IP address of Lab Hosts (10.0.0.1-254) will not be translated to the Lab Router's WAN IP address (172.16.0.2), giving visibility on who sent the traffic and where traffic is going to. Implemented logrotate to compress and rotate logs daily/weekly to keep logs at manageable size. This allows older logs to be cleaned automatically ensuring new logs can be stored on the firewall. Managing Firewall and DNS logs I matched the log prefix NFT-[ACTION]-[CHAIN]-[ACTION] that was established on iptables.conf. By matching the first 4 characters, I can make a separate nftables.log file for the nftables log. Without this, firewall logs would be mixed along with other kernel logs in dmesg -w. While the logs with tags dnsmasq_log are set to dns.log. 1 # 1. Capture Firewall logs 2 :msg, contains, "NFT-" /var/log/nftables.log 3 & stop 4 5 # 2. Capture DNS queries 6 if ($syslogtag == 'dnsmasq_log') then { 7 /var/log/dns.log 8 stop 9 } 10 The dnsmasq_log are assigned by importing imfile on rsyslog. While it might seem redundant as all dnsmasq.log are being stored on dns.log, it allows us to easily add a new DNS service that generate logs into the pipeline. 23 module(load="imfile") 24 25 input(type="imfile" 26 File="/var/log/dnsmasq.log" 27 Tag="dnsmasq_log" 28 Severity="info" 29 Facility="local0") File: /etc/rsyslog.conf Since its likely that DNS logs would be a lot more, I set the the dns.log to rotate daily and only store up to 7 log archives at once. While nftables.log is only set to rotate weekly and store 4 log archives at once.
File: /etc/logrotate.d/firewall
Established a consistent addressing and naming scheme which makes future firewall rule management easier. Assigning readable and intuitive names as well as setting lab network to 10.x.x.x, 172.x.x.x for infrastructure, and leaving the 192.x.x.x for external hosts. Standardized Interface Names and Network Addresses I first identified the MAC Addresses of the interface with ip addr, then changed their NAME= value on udev config. File: /etc/udev/rules.d/70-persistent-net.rules In line 30, I added a route to LabNetwork (10.0.0.0/24) via firewall's lan0 (172.16.0.1) interface. Without this route, traffic going to LabNetwork (10.0.0.0/24) will be forwarded to 192.168.11.1 (gateway). ... 7 8 auto lo 9 iface lo inet loopback 10 11 # LAN - (Ethernet) 12 auto lan0 13 iface lan0 inet static 14 address 172.16.0.1 15 netmask 255.255.255.0 16 17 # WAN (Wireless) 18 auto wan0 19 iface wan0 inet static 20 address 192.168.11.200 21 netmask 255.255.255.0 22 gateway 192.168.11.1 23 dns-nameservers 8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4 24 25 26 27 wpa-conf /etc/wpa_supplicant/wpa_supplicant.conf 28 29 # Route to LAB network 30 up ip route add 10.0.0.0/24 via 172.16.0.2 dev lan0 File: /etc/network/interfaces Based on the test summary below, nftables and dnsmasq implementation is working as expected.Input Chain Tests A. Accessing blocked domain chess.com
output: $ nslookup chess.com Server: UnKnown Address: 172.16.0.1 *** UnKnown can't find chess.com: No response from server dns log: 2026-06-17T21:05:27.351505+08:00 firewall dnsmasq_log Jun 17 21:05:27 dnsmasq[4579]: query[A] chess.com from 10.0.0.50 2026-06-17T21:05:27.351547+08:00 firewall dnsmasq_log Jun 17 21:05:27 dnsmasq[4579]: config chess.com is NXDOMAIN 2026-06-17T21:05:27.354389+08:00 firewall dnsmasq_log Jun 17 21:05:27 dnsmasq[4579]: query[AAAA] chess.com from 10.0.0.50 2026-06-17T21:05:27.354447+08:00 firewall dnsmasq_log Jun 17 21:05:27 dnsmasq[4579]: config chess.com is NXDOMAIN Disabling NAT offers more visibility on hosts but add complexity to the network configurations as static routes need to be specified on the gateways. DNS logs provides insights on hosts activity but also introduces massive log volume which requires proper log retention and filtering important considerations. Accurate time synchronization is essential for event correlation on multi-host systems. The higher the differences in time, the harder it is to correlate events and get insights. DNS filtering compliments L3/L4 filtering. Many modern website are being tunneled or delivered via the massive IP blocks of companies like Cloudflare. Setup Wazuh server for centralized log collection and to monitor lab hosts. Setup windows server and vulnerable hosts inside the lab. Attack the vulnerable hosts inside the lab.
